nodes.label: Entanglement
nodes.title: Entanglement
nodes.statement: A composite state is entangled when it cannot be written as a mixture of product states. Everything on this map asks one of four things about that definition: how do we recognise such a state, how much entanglement does it hold, what can it be turned into, and what changes when more than two parties share it?

nodes.label: Detection
nodes.title: Detection
nodes.statement: Given a density matrix, is it entangled? The definition asks us to search over every possible mixture of product states, so the branch looks for tests we can actually run, and asks how far they can reach.

nodes.label: Measures
nodes.title: Measures
nodes.statement: How much entanglement does a state hold? For pure bipartite states the answer is essentially unique. For mixed states, different operational questions give different quantities, and many of them resist calculation.

nodes.label: Conversion
nodes.title: Conversion
nodes.statement: What can one entangled state be turned into, using only local operations and classical communication (LOCC)? Conversion treats entanglement as a resource, and most of its hardest open questions concern noisy states that resist distillation.

nodes.label: Multipartite
nodes.title: Multipartite entanglement
nodes.statement: What changes when three or more parties share a state? There is no longer one maximally entangled state to aim for, and the classification of states grows quickly with the number of parties.

nodes.label: Separable states are PPT
nodes.title: Every separable state has a positive partial transpose
nodes.statement: Transpose one subsystem of a separable state and the result still has no negative eigenvalues. A negative eigenvalue is therefore proof of entanglement, and this test is stronger than Bell inequalities.

nodes.label: PPT decides 2×2 and 2×3
nodes.title: In 2×2 and 2×3 systems, PPT is equivalent to separability
nodes.statement: In these two smallest cases the partial transpose test is both necessary and sufficient. Separability is settled by one eigenvalue calculation.

nodes.label: PPT entangled states exist
nodes.title: PPT entangled states exist in 3×3 and 2×4
nodes.statement: One dimension past the solved cases, the equivalence fails: there are entangled states the partial transpose test cannot see. Explicit examples come from a separate criterion based on the range of the density matrix.

nodes.label: Witnesses detect entanglement
nodes.title: Entanglement can be certified by witness operators
nodes.statement: A witness is an observable whose expectation value can only take certain values on separable states, so measuring beyond them certifies entanglement. A Bell inequality violation can be written formally as such a witness.

nodes.label: Realignment criterion
nodes.title: The cross norm and realignment criterion
nodes.statement: For a separable state, the singular values of a realigned density matrix sum to at most 1. The test is easy to compute. It is necessary for separability but not in general sufficient.

nodes.label: A complete test hierarchy
nodes.title: A hierarchy of semidefinite tests detects every entangled state
nodes.statement: Separable states have symmetric extensions to more parties. Searching for such an extension is a semidefinite program, and any entangled state fails at some finite level of the hierarchy. The first level is the partial transpose test.

nodes.label: Separability is NP-hard
nodes.title: Deciding separability is NP-hard
nodes.statement: Gurvits proved hardness for states within an inverse exponential distance of the separable set. Gharibian extended it to an inverse polynomial distance. So no efficient general test is expected unless P = NP, which is consistent with the hierarchy above having no fixed cut-off level.

nodes.label: PPT² conjecture
nodes.title: Is the composition of two PPT maps always entanglement breaking?
nodes.statement: Equivalently: can two PPT entangled links ever generate entanglement between their ends through entanglement swapping? The conjecture says no.
nodes.unknown: It has been proved in dimension 3 and for Gaussian channels. Higher finite dimensions remain open.

nodes.label: How powerful is QMA(2)?
nodes.title: How powerful are two unentangled quantum proofs?
nodes.statement: QMA(2) allows a verifier two proofs guaranteed to be unentangled. Harrow and Montanaro showed that two proofs can simulate many, and tied the log-sized version of QMA(2) to separability testing.
nodes.unknown: Only the trivial bounds QMA ⊆ QMA(2) ⊆ NEXP are known. If proofs are restricted to non-negative amplitudes the class equals NEXP at suitable constant gaps, but that does not yet transfer to QMA(2) without gap amplification.

nodes.label: Measures must be monotones
nodes.title: A measure must not increase under local operations
nodes.statement: Vidal characterised the functions that do not increase on average under LOCC. For bipartite pure states, a single number is not enough to capture everything about single-copy conversion.

nodes.label: Pure states: entropy is unique
nodes.title: When a measure must equal the reduced entropy on pure states
nodes.statement: The uniqueness theorem gives necessary and sufficient conditions for a measure to coincide with the von Neumann entropy of the reduced state on pure states. For this case, the question of how much has one answer.

nodes.label: Two-qubit formation formula
nodes.title: Entanglement of formation has a closed form for two qubits
nodes.statement: Wootters proved an explicit formula for the entanglement of formation of any two-qubit state. Outside this case, computing it generally means optimising over decompositions.

nodes.label: Formation is additive
nodes.title: Entanglement of formation is additive
nodes.statement: This conjecture is false. Shor showed it stands or falls with additivity of minimum output entropy and of the Holevo capacity, and Hastings then showed superadditivity of communication capacity with entangled inputs.

nodes.label: Cost is regularised formation
nodes.title: Entanglement cost equals regularised entanglement of formation
nodes.statement: The asymptotic cost of preparing a state equals its entanglement of formation per copy, in the limit of many copies. The formula is exact but involves a limit that is hard to evaluate.

nodes.label: Negativity is computable
nodes.title: Negativity and log-negativity can be computed for any state
nodes.statement: These quantities come directly from the partial transpose, and bound teleportation capacity and distillable entanglement. Log-negativity does not increase on average under PPT operations, even though it is not convex.

nodes.label: Relative entropy is additive
nodes.title: Relative entropy of entanglement is additive
nodes.statement: The relative entropy of entanglement measures distance to the separable set. Vollbrecht and Werner found a counterexample to its additivity, which is why the regularised version is the quantity that appears in asymptotic theorems.

nodes.label: Squashed entanglement is faithful
nodes.title: Squashed entanglement is additive and faithful
nodes.statement: Defined from conditional mutual information minimised over extensions, it is an entanglement monotone and a lower bound on entanglement of formation. It is strictly positive exactly on entangled states.

nodes.label: Formula for distillable entanglement?
nodes.title: Can distillable entanglement be computed in general?
nodes.statement: The one-way rate has a coding theorem, but it is a regularised optimisation over many copies.
nodes.unknown: Single-letter formulas are known only in special classes, such as degradable and PPT states, with new non-degradable families added in 2026. No general tractable formula is known, so most work goes into bounds.

nodes.label: Pure states concentrate
nodes.title: Partly entangled pure states concentrate into singlets
nodes.statement: With many copies of a partly entangled pure state, local operations can produce a smaller number of maximally entangled pairs, and this is what gives the entropy its operational meaning.

nodes.label: Majorization decides pure LOCC
nodes.title: Majorization decides single-copy pure state conversion
nodes.statement: Nielsen's theorem gives necessary and sufficient conditions for converting one bipartite pure state into another by LOCC, in terms of a partial order on their Schmidt coefficients.

nodes.label: Catalysts enable conversions
nodes.title: Entangled catalysts enable otherwise impossible conversions
nodes.statement: An extra entangled state can make a forbidden pure state transformation possible, and be returned unchanged at the end.

nodes.label: Entropy rules catalysed conversion
nodes.title: With catalysts, entanglement entropy decides pure state conversion
nodes.statement: Allow entangled catalysts, and entanglement entropy completely characterises state transformations of bipartite pure states. This gives the asymptotic quantity an operational meaning in a single copy.

nodes.label: Noisy pairs can be distilled
nodes.title: Noisy entanglement can be purified by LOCC
nodes.statement: From many sufficiently pure noisy pairs, two parties can extract fewer pairs of arbitrarily high fidelity, then use them for teleportation. Distillation protocols are also tied directly to quantum error correction.

nodes.label: All two-qubit entanglement distills
nodes.title: Every entangled two-qubit state is distillable
nodes.statement: Local filtering followed by purification works on any inseparable 2×2 state. In this smallest case, entanglement and distillability coincide.

nodes.label: PPT entanglement can't be distilled
nodes.title: Bound entanglement exists
nodes.statement: A distillable state must violate the partial transpose test, so PPT entangled states cannot be distilled. There are two kinds of entanglement: free and bound.

nodes.label: Bound entanglement can be activated
nodes.title: Bound entanglement can improve teleportation
nodes.statement: Undistillable alone, bound entanglement can raise the teleportation fidelity of a single free entangled pair above what that pair can reach unaided.

nodes.label: Do NPT bound states exist?
nodes.title: Do bound entangled states with a negative partial transpose exist?
nodes.statement: Every distillable state is NPT. Is the converse true? In dimensions above 2×2, evidence going back to 1999 suggests some NPT states may be undistillable, with Werner states the central family under study.
nodes.unknown: It remains listed among the five open problems of Horodecki, Rudnicki and Życzkowski, and a 2024 paper still calls it long-standing. A 2006 preprint claimed existence, but later work continues to treat the question as open.

nodes.label: Two copies of NPT Werner fail
nodes.title: NPT Werner states are two-copy undistillable in every dimension
nodes.statement: A July 2026 preprint proves a partial-trace inequality for matrices of rank at most two. It applies this to claim two-copy undistillability of NPT Werner states in arbitrary local dimension.
nodes.unknown: No independent confirmation had been found by the check date. Even if correct, it covers two copies, while the existence of NPT bound entanglement needs every number of copies.

nodes.label: Bell nonlocality implies distillable
nodes.title: Bell nonlocality implies distillability (the Peres conjecture)
nodes.statement: Peres conjectured in 1999 that the two were equivalent. Vértesi and Brunner gave a bound entangled state that violates a Bell inequality, so nonlocality implies neither distillability nor a negative partial transpose.

nodes.label: LOCC is irreversible
nodes.title: Entanglement manipulation under LOCC is irreversible
nodes.statement: Creating a bound entangled state costs entanglement, yet none can be distilled back. Every entangled state has strictly positive entanglement cost, so this happens for all non-distillable entangled states.

nodes.label: Non-entangling ops are reversible
nodes.title: Entanglement is reversible under all non-entangling operations
nodes.statement: Lami and Regula showed this is false: entanglement theory is irreversible under all non-entangling transformations, so reversibility would need a macroscopic amount of entanglement generated along the way, by certain measures.

nodes.label: Generalised Stein's lemma
nodes.title: The generalised quantum Stein's lemma, and reversibility under asymptotically non-entangling operations
nodes.statement: The Stein exponent for testing an entangled state against separable states equals the regularised relative entropy of entanglement. This gives reversibility when operations may generate vanishing entanglement. The original 2010 proof had a gap, found in 2022. Hayashi and Yamasaki, and Lami, then gave independent proofs in 2024, and the Hayashi–Yamasaki proof has been formalised in Lean.

nodes.label: Catalysts can't free PPT bound
nodes.title: Catalysis cannot distill PPT bound entanglement
nodes.statement: Catalytic transformations can never distill entanglement from a PPT bound entangled state, even if the catalyst becomes correlated with the system. So catalysis cannot make entanglement theory asymptotically reversible.

nodes.label: Three qubits: GHZ and W
nodes.title: Three qubits can be entangled in two inequivalent ways
nodes.statement: Under stochastic LOCC, fully entangled three-qubit pure states fall into two classes that cannot be converted into one another, represented by the GHZ and W states.

nodes.label: Four qubits: nine families
nodes.title: Four qubits fall into nine families
nodes.statement: The classification of pure four-qubit states under stochastic LOCC yields nine families, some of them with continuous parameters.

nodes.label: Qubit entanglement is monogamous
nodes.title: Entanglement between qubits is monogamous
nodes.statement: How much A shares with B limits how much it can share with C. Coffman, Kundu and Wootters proved this for three qubits, and Osborne and Verstraete proved the conjectured inequality for any number of qubits.

nodes.label: Maximally entangled sets
nodes.title: No single maximally entangled multipartite state exists
nodes.statement: Since no one state plays this role, de Vicente, Spee and Kraus define a maximally entangled set. They determine it for three and four qubits. It is infinite in both cases, of measure zero for three qubits, and includes almost all four-qubit states.

nodes.label: Almost all states are isolated
nodes.title: Almost all multipartite pure states are isolated under LOCC
nodes.statement: Generic states have no nontrivial local symmetry. As a result, nontrivial deterministic LOCC transformations among generic fully entangled states are almost never possible.

nodes.label: Bound states can superactivate
nodes.title: Two bound entangled states can together be distillable
nodes.statement: In a multi-party setting, two non-distillable states tensored together can form a distillable state, a true superadditivity of distillable entanglement.

nodes.label: Network entanglement
nodes.title: Standard genuine multipartite entanglement can be built from pairs
nodes.statement: A source that only distributes bipartite entanglement can produce genuinely k-partite entangled states for any k. Navascués et al. therefore propose genuine network entanglement as a stricter definition, with witnesses.

nodes.label: Which AME states exist?
nodes.title: For which parties and dimensions do AME states exist?
nodes.statement: An AME state is maximally mixed on every reduction to half of its parties or fewer. None exists for seven qubits, and four six-level systems, an open problem until 2021, do have one.
nodes.unknown: Existence is a case-by-case question across n and d. One 2026 preprint names AME(8,4) as the first remaining open case, assuming the seven-party result below holds.

nodes.label: AME(7,d) exists for all d ≥ 3
nodes.title: Seven-party AME states exist exactly when d ≥ 3
nodes.statement: An August 2026 preprint constructs states for all odd dimensions and for dimensions congruent to 2 modulo 4, completing the classification for up to seven parties together with earlier results.
nodes.unknown: No independent confirmation had been found by the check date.

nodes.label: Asymptotic tensor restriction
nodes.title: When can many copies of one tensor produce another?
nodes.statement: Multipartite pure states are tensors, so asymptotic conversion meets Strassen's programme on matrix multiplication. Quantum functionals gave the first nontrivial universal spectral points after thirty years, and connect to the quantum marginal problem and entanglement polytopes.
nodes.unknown: Quantum functionals give some spectral points, not a full solution of the asymptotic restriction problem.
